brief.metaDescription: See 7 of the best running shoes for beginners in 2026, with prices, pros, cons and who should skip each, plus how to pick your first pair.
brief.searchIntent: The searcher is ready to buy a first pair of running shoes and wants a short ranked list with clear reasons, prices and who each shoe suits. A listicle with a quick comparison and a simple way to choose serves this best.
brief.reader: A new or casual runner shopping online who knows little shoe jargon, may be starting with a walk to run plan or a first 5K, and wants to pick one pair and buy with confidence. Next they want to check fit and price, then buy.
brief.angle: We rank seven shoes in plain words, say who should skip each one, and show prices with the source and date so new runners do not have to decode lab scores. We also keep the list to shoes built for beginners, unlike pages that mix in race shoes.

outline.h2: How we picked these beginner running shoes
points: Say plainly that Stride Running picks from published tests and buyer guides, and name the test sites: RTINGS, RunRepeat, Fleet Feet and Run Weekly.
List the picking checks in plain words: cushioning, stability, true to size fit, weight, price and whether the shoe feels good with no break-in.
Explain that beginners should look for a cushioned daily trainer and skip carbon plated race shoes.

outline.h2: 1. ASICS Novablast 6: best overall for new runners
points: What it does well: RTINGS calls it the best beginner shoe it tested, with cushioning that protects your legs as you get used to regular training.
Numbers in plain words: cushioning 8.5, stability 7.1 and true to size 9.4, with a weight of 247.7 g (8.74 oz) and a heel stack of 41.9 mm.
Pros: wide sizing is available, it is light enough for regular runs, and it can cover a first 5K or 10K.
Pricing: the sources give no price, so use the current Stride Running price or flag it for the editor.
Who should skip it: runners who want a lot of structure, since the stability score of 7.1 sits just above the 7.0 mark RTINGS calls decent.

outline.h2: 2. Brooks Ghost 17: best for a classic daily trainer
points: What it does well: it is a top pick in Fleet Feet's list and named as a neutral shoe most beginners start in.
Run Weekly says Brooks has been reliable for new runners in the author's experience, so use that as one tester's view.
Pros: a neutral daily trainer that suits most beginners who do not overpronate.
Pricing: no price in the sources, so the editor must add a current price.
Who should skip it: runners whose ankles collapse inward a lot, who may do better in a stability shoe.

outline.h2: 3. HOKA Clifton 10: best for soft, cushioned miles
points: What it does well: Run Weekly calls it Hoka's most popular daily trainer and says the compression-moulded EVA foam absorbs impact well.
Pros: soft cushioning that does not feel clunky, and it appears in Fleet Feet's top 10 and in Shoe Station's neutral picks.
Cons and who should skip it: anyone who wants a firmer ground feel, since the sources describe soft cushioning.
Pricing: no price in the sources, so the editor must add one.

outline.h2: 4. adidas Adizero Evo SL: best for one shoe that does it all
points: What it does well: Run Weekly says it suits easy days, tempo runs and most things between, so a beginner can own one pair.

Who should skip it: runners who need support, because RunRepeat says the narrow midsole and minimal support suit neutral runners only.

blocks.text: This guide ranks seven of the **best running shoes for beginners** in plain words, with who each one suits and who should skip it. If you're standing in front of a wall of shoes or scrolling through dozens of tabs, we want your first purchase to feel easier than your first run.

Most guides lean on lab terms that mean little when you're new, and some mix in race shoes that don't suit a beginner at all. We pulled from published tests at [RTINGS](https://www.rtings.com/running-shoes/reviews/best/beginners), [RunRepeat](https://runrepeat.com/guides/best-for-beginners-running-shoes), [Fleet Feet](https://www.fleetfeet.com/running-shoe-buyers-guide) and [Run Weekly](https://www.runweekly.com/best-running-shoes-for-beginners/), and we name the model version each one tested.
To get the most from it, you can follow these steps:

items: Read the seven picks and note who each shoe suits and who should skip it.
Check the fit tips at the end of the guide.
Choose one pair and buy with confidence.

sections.h2: How we picked these beginner running shoes

blocks.text: Stride Running doesn't test shoes in a lab ourselves, so we pick from published tests and buyer guides and explain the results in plain words for new runners. For this list, we drew on [RTINGS](https://www.rtings.com/running-shoes/reviews/best/beginners), [RunRepeat](https://runrepeat.com/guides/best-for-beginners-running-shoes), [Fleet Feet](https://www.fleetfeet.com/running-shoe-buyers-guide) and [Run Weekly](https://www.runweekly.com/best-running-shoes-for-beginners/), and we also read [Shoe Station's beginner guide](https://www.shoestation.com/blog/2026-running-shoes-for-beginners).
Here's how we narrowed the field. We looked for the same checks across those sources, and we explain each one in everyday words so you can use it when you shop.

items: Cushioning is how well the shoe absorbs each landing, so hard ground feels less harsh on your legs, and [RTINGS](https://www.rtings.com/running-shoes/reviews/best/beginners) treats a score of 7.5 or higher as good.
Stability is how controlled the shoe feels when you land and push off, and RTINGS counts a score of 7.0 or higher as decent.
True to size fit tells you whether your usual running size is a safe starting point, and RTINGS says a score of 9 or higher suggests it is.
Weight matters because most beginners want a shoe that is [supportive and cushioned without feeling like a brick](https://www.runweekly.com/best-running-shoes-for-beginners/) on their feet.
Price counts too, since [you do not need the most expensive shoe to start](https://www.shoestation.com/blog/2026-running-shoes-for-beginners).
Comfort from the first run matters, because a good running shoe should have [no break-in period](https://www.shoestation.com/blog/2026-running-shoes-for-beginners).

blocks.text: We also kept the list to shoes built for new runners, since [RunRepeat](https://runrepeat.com/guides/best-for-beginners-running-shoes) says carbon plates are not good for beginners and points new runners toward a cushioned daily trainer instead. A **daily trainer** is a comfortable everyday shoe you can use for most of your runs, so that is what you'll find below.
Shoe models update often, so we say which version each source tested. If you want a wider view first, [our running shoe guide](https://striderunning.example/guides/running-shoes) covers the basics.

sections.h2: 1. ASICS Novablast 6: best overall for new runners

blocks.text: ASICS Novablast 6 is a cushioned daily running shoe from ASICS that suits new runners who want comfort from the first mile. [RTINGS calls it the best running shoe for beginners it has tested](https://www.rtings.com/running-shoes/reviews/best/beginners), so it earns our top spot.

The big strength is cushioning that does an excellent job of protecting your legs from impact as you get used to regular training. We think that matters a lot in a first pair, because your legs are still adapting to the pounding of each run.
Here are the RTINGS numbers, in plain words:

items: [Cushioning scores 8.5](https://www.rtings.com/running-shoes/reviews/best/beginners), which is above the 7.5 mark RTINGS calls good.
[Stability scores 7.1](https://www.rtings.com/running-shoes/reviews/best/beginners), which sits just above the 7.0 mark RTINGS calls decent.
[True to size scores 9.4](https://www.rtings.com/running-shoes/reviews/best/beginners), so your usual running size is a safe place to start.
[The shoe weighs 247.7 g (8.74 oz) with a heel stack height of 41.9 mm](https://www.rtings.com/running-shoes/reviews/best/beginners), and heel stack height is how much shoe sits under your heel.

blocks.text: Why it works: [RTINGS says it is light enough that it doesn't feel cumbersome on regular runs](https://www.rtings.com/running-shoes/reviews/best/beginners), and the cushioning gives back a decent amount of energy as you push off. That helps faster running feel less labored as you gain confidence.
Here's what it offers you, and you can look for the same things when you shop other [road running shoes](https://striderunning.example/shoes/road):

items: Wide sizing is available, so check the width options if your feet need more room.
It can cover your regular runs and a first 5K or 10K, especially if your goal is to finish comfortably.
You won't need to upgrade right away, since it stays capable as your runs get longer and you pick up the pace.

blocks.text: Price: the sources we used don't list one, so check the current Stride Running price on the shoe page before you buy. [RTINGS links to several shops for current prices](https://www.rtings.com/running-shoes/reviews/best/beginners) if you want to compare.

Who should skip it: runners who want a lot of structure underfoot. Its stability score of 7.1 is only just above the 7.0 decent mark, so if you want more control, the stability pick later in this list may suit you better.

sections.h2: 2. Brooks Ghost 17: best for a classic daily trainer

blocks.text: Brooks Ghost 17 is a running shoe from Brooks that works as a neutral daily trainer for easy, regular miles.

[Shoe Station](https://www.shoestation.com/blog/2026-running-shoes-for-beginners) names the Brooks Ghost as a top pick for neutral running shoes, the type it says most beginners start with. Those shoes are versatile and give even cushioning without extra structural inserts, so your foot can move naturally.

The author at Run Weekly, who offers one tester's view, says that [Brooks, Hoka and Saucony have been reliable for new runners](https://www.runweekly.com/best-running-shoes-for-beginners/), at least in their experience, so treat that as one person's opinion alongside the other guides.
Here's what the sources tell us about why it suits a first pair:

items: It is a neutral daily trainer, which is where most beginners start.
It suits new runners who do not overpronate, meaning their ankles do not collapse inward much when they walk or run.

blocks.text: Price: the sources we used don't list one for this shoe, so check the current Stride Running price on the shoe page before you buy, since prices change by shop and by week.

Who should skip it: runners whose ankles collapse inward a lot. Shoe Station says a stability shoe can help in that case, because it uses [firmer foam or guide rails on the inside of the arch](https://www.shoestation.com/blog/2026-running-shoes-for-beginners) to keep your stride lined up.
If you notice your ankles rolling inward on your walks or runs, look at the stability pick later in this list, and if they don't, a neutral shoe like the Ghost 17 is a sensible place to begin.

sections.h2: 3. HOKA Clifton 10: best for soft, cushioned miles

blocks.text: HOKA Clifton 10 is a running shoe from Hoka that works as a soft, cushioned daily trainer for road miles.

Run Weekly says the soft feel doesn't come across as clunky, and that the compression-moulded EVA foam does a great job of absorbing impact, which is what new runners need as they build up their mileage.
It also shows up on more than one buying list, and you can find it in these places:

items: It is one of the ten shoes in [Fleet Feet's best running shoes list](https://www.fleetfeet.com/running-shoe-buyers-guide), which covers every type of runner.
It is named among the neutral picks in [Shoe Station's beginner guide](https://www.shoestation.com/blog/2026-running-shoes-for-beginners), alongside the Brooks Ghost and the ASICS Gel Nimbus.

blocks.text: Because Shoe Station lists it as a neutral shoe, it fits the group most beginners start in, and neutral shoes give even cushioning without extra structure so your foot can move in its natural way.

Price: the sources we used don't list one for this shoe, so check the current Stride Running price on the shoe page before you buy. Prices change by shop and by week, so a quick look right before you order is worth the minute.

Who should skip it? Surprisingly, this comes down to how you like the ground to feel, because the sources describe soft cushioning and you may enjoy a different shoe on this list more if you want a firmer, more connected feel underfoot.
If your ankles collapse inward a lot when you walk or run, Shoe Station suggests a stability shoe instead.

sections.h2: 4. adidas Adizero Evo SL: best for one shoe that does it all

blocks.text: The adidas Adizero Evo SL is a running shoe from adidas that is built to handle easy days, faster tempo runs and most things in between. [Run Weekly](https://www.runweekly.com/best-running-shoes-for-beginners/) says that range is ideal for beginners who want one solid pair instead of a whole rotation.
Here's why it works for new runners, based on what the two sources say:

items: It uses Lightstrike Pro foam, which Run Weekly says gives a nice mix of comfort and pop, soft enough for longer runs with a bit of bounce when you push the pace.
It weighs 7.9 oz (223 g), and [RunRepeat](https://runrepeat.com/guides/best-running-shoes) says that minimal build adds to its effortless feel.
Run Weekly's tester put about 50 miles on a pair and says they are holding up nicely.

blocks.text: Price: Run Weekly lists the Evo SL at £120, which the author calls pretty good value. RunRepeat showed a $150 list price with a $65 deal at Shoebacca when it wrote its guide, so prices move and it's worth checking the current Stride Running price before you buy.
RunRepeat lists a few things to know before you order:

items: The toebox may wear out sooner than the rest of the shoe.

blocks.text: Who should skip it? RunRepeat says the narrow midsole and minimal support make the Evo SL ideal only for neutral runners, so if you need more structure, a stability shoe will suit you better.

sections.h2: 5. PUMA Velocity Nitro 5: best for grip and bounce

blocks.text: PUMA Velocity Nitro 5 is a running shoe from PUMA that is built as a daily trainer for people who are building their miles. [RunRepeat names it the best running shoe for beginners overall](https://runrepeat.com/guides/best-for-beginners-running-shoes), saying it has the comfort, grippy control and bounce a new runner needs.
Here's how RunRepeat's lab numbers look in plain words, and why they matter when you're building up your miles:

items: Flexibility: in a 30 degree bend test, the shoe is [40% more flexible than average](https://runrepeat.com/guides/best-for-beginners-running-shoes), which RunRepeat says keeps the ride natural and enjoyable for beginners.
Wet grip: the PUMAGRIP rubber outsole scored 0.78 in RunRepeat's wet-condition test, so you can expect steady footing if you meet wet pavement or rain.

Bounce: energy return was [64.0% in the heel and 69.3% in the forefoot](https://runrepeat.com/guides/best-for-beginners-running-shoes), which means the foam gives back a good share of the energy you put in.

blocks.text: As you can see, those numbers add up to a shoe with good bounce and wet grip, and RunRepeat also notes a secure lockdown and good durability from top to bottom.

Price: [RunRepeat shows a $140 list price](https://runrepeat.com/guides/best-for-beginners-running-shoes), with $102 listed through KICKS CREW when it wrote its guide. Prices change from shop to shop, so check the current Stride Running price before you buy.

Who should skip it? This comes down to your stride, because RunRepeat describes the Velocity Nitro 5 as a neutral shoe and advises runners with overpronation or added stability concerns to choose a more structured trainer. If your ankles tend to roll inward, look at the stability pick further down this list before you decide.

sections.h2: 6. ASICS GT-1000 15: best for extra stability

blocks.text: The ASICS GT-1000 15 is a stability running shoe from ASICS that [RunRepeat picks as the best stability shoe for beginners](https://runrepeat.com/guides/best-for-beginners-running-shoes). If you want a shoe that keeps your stride steady while you build up your miles, it's a good one to try.

What does stability mean here? If your ankles collapse inward when you walk or run, which is called **overpronation**, a [stability shoe can help by using firmer foam or guide rails on the inside of the arch](https://www.shoestation.com/blog/2026-running-shoes-for-beginners) to keep your stride lined up.
You can browse our full range of [stability running shoes](https://striderunning.example/shoes/stability) if you'd like to compare this pick with other supportive models.

Price: RunRepeat shows a [$115 list price, with $100 listed at Running Warehouse](https://runrepeat.com/guides/best-for-beginners-running-shoes) when it wrote its guide. Prices change from shop to shop, so check the current Stride Running price before you buy.
Here's how to tell whether this shoe suits you:

items: Choose it if your ankles roll inward a lot when you walk or run and you want a shoe that keeps your stride lined up.
Choose it if you're starting out and want a stability shoe that testers have picked as a good first pair.
Skip it if you have a neutral gait, because you'll likely feel better in one of the neutral shoes higher up this list.
Skip it if you're not sure which type you are, and check how your ankles move before you decide.

blocks.text: Surprisingly, most beginners do well in neutral shoes, and [Shoe Station notes that most new runners start there](https://www.shoestation.com/blog/2026-running-shoes-for-beginners).

sections.h2: 7. adidas Questar 4: best on a budget

blocks.text: adidas Questar 4 is a running shoe from adidas that [RTINGS names the best budget pick for beginners](https://www.rtings.com/running-shoes/reviews/best/beginners) that can still handle regular running. We like it as a starting point if price matters to you.
Here's how its numbers look in plain words, based on [RTINGS test results](https://www.rtings.com/running-shoes/reviews/best/beginners):

items: Cushioning scores 7.0, which tells you how well the shoe softens each landing on hard surfaces.
Stability scores 8.1, which tells you how controlled the shoe feels when you land and push off.
True to size scores 9.3, so you can usually start with your normal running shoe size.
It weighs 305.5 g (10.78 oz), and the heel stack height is 38.2 mm.

blocks.text: Why it works: the stability score of 8.1 is higher than the 7.1 that [RTINGS gave the ASICS Novablast 6](https://www.rtings.com/running-shoes/reviews/best/beginners). If you feel wobbly while you get used to running, that extra control can help you feel more confident.
This table puts the two shoes side by side so you can compare the scores and details that matter most.

As you can see, the Questar 4 has less cushioning and weighs more than the Novablast 6, and [RTINGS lists no wide sizing](https://www.rtings.com/running-shoes/reviews/best/beginners) for it. If you have wider feet or want the softest ride, you may prefer a shoe higher up this list.

Price: our sources don't give a price for this shoe, so check the current Stride Running price before you buy. If a lower price is your main goal right now, the Questar 4 is the budget pick RTINGS recommends for regular running.

sections.h2: How to choose your first pair

blocks.text: You can pick your first pair in three steps: decide between a neutral and a stability shoe, check the fit, then set your budget. Here's how each step works, so you can buy with confidence.
Neutral or stability?
[Most beginners start in neutral shoes](https://www.shoestation.com/blog/2026-running-shoes-for-beginners), which give even cushioning and let your foot move naturally.

If your ankles collapse inward a lot when you walk or run, a stability shoe may suit you better. [Shoe Station explains](https://www.shoestation.com/blog/2026-running-shoes-for-beginners) that these use firmer foam or guide rails on the inside of the arch to keep your stride lined up.
Check the fit

Once you know which type of shoe you want, take a few minutes to check the fit, and our guide on [how running shoes should fit](https://striderunning.example/guides/shoe-fit) goes into more detail. These checks come from our sources:

items: Leave about a thumb's width between your toes and the front of the shoe, because [your feet swell as they warm up during a run](https://www.shoestation.com/blog/2026-running-shoes-for-beginners).
Expect comfort from the first run, since [proper running shoes should not need a break-in period](https://www.runweekly.com/best-running-shoes-for-beginners/).
Remember that [your running shoe size may differ from your everyday size](https://www.rtings.com/running-shoes/reviews/best/beginners), so don't assume the two match.

blocks.text: Budget and shoe life

You don't need the most expensive shoe to start. [Shoe Station notes](https://www.shoestation.com/blog/2026-running-shoes-for-beginners) that many entry level models give beginners everything they need at a friendlier price.

A useful question to ask is how long a pair will last you. [Shoe Station says](https://www.shoestation.com/blog/2026-running-shoes-for-beginners) to expect about 300 to 500 miles from a quality pair, which usually means six to nine months if you run three times a week, and our guide on [how long running shoes last](https://striderunning.example/blog/running-shoe-lifespan) shows what to look for as a pair wears out.
These two kinds of shoe are worth skipping at the start:

items: Skip flat lifestyle sneakers, because [they lack the impact absorbing foam and support you need for running](https://www.shoestation.com/blog/2026-running-shoes-for-beginners).

Skip carbon plated race shoes, because [RunRepeat says carbon plates are not good for beginners](https://runrepeat.com/guides/best-for-beginners-running-shoes) and a cushioned daily trainer is the better place to begin.

blocks.text: Next, pick one shoe from the list above and browse road shoes at Stride Running, then use our [how running shoes should fit](https://striderunning.example/guides/shoe-fit) guide to check your size before you buy. After that, our [first 5K plan](https://striderunning.example/guides/first-5k) shows you how to build up your miles.
Should running shoes be a little tight at first?

No. Shoes should feel good from your very first run with no break-in period, and [Shoe Station](https://www.shoestation.com/blog/2026-running-shoes-for-beginners) says that if they don't feel great when you lace them up, they aren't the right pair.
You also want about a thumb's width of space between your toes and the end of the shoe, because your feet swell as they warm up.
How do I choose my first running shoes?

[Shoe Station](https://www.shoestation.com/blog/2026-running-shoes-for-beginners) says most beginners begin in neutral shoes, so start by deciding between a neutral shoe and a stability shoe. Our how to choose section above walks you through each step.

items: Decide between a neutral shoe and a stability shoe.
Check the fit.
Pick the cushioning and budget that suit you.

blocks.text: What Nike shoes are good for beginner runners?
[RunRepeat](https://runrepeat.com/guides/best-for-beginners-running-shoes) also picks two other Nike shoes for beginners:

items: The Nike Revolution 8 is its best budget choice.

blocks.text: Do I need expensive shoes to start running?

No. [Shoe Station](https://www.shoestation.com/blog/2026-running-shoes-for-beginners) says many entry level models from major brands give beginners everything they need at a lower price. A comfortable, cushioned daily trainer is a better place to start than a high-end shoe with advanced foam.
How long will my first pair of running shoes last?

[Shoe Station](https://www.shoestation.com/blog/2026-running-shoes-for-beginners) says to expect about 300 to 500 miles from a quality pair. For most beginners running three times a week, that works out to about six to nine months before you need a new pair.
